sections.heading: 3.1 Maximal update parametrization (\mu\mathsf{P})
sections.text: \mu\mathsf{P} ( Yang and Hu, 2021 ) refers to scaling paradigms for weight initialization and optimizer configurations such that for any fixed training step t and fixed model depth L, as the model width n\to\infty, \forall\ell\in[L], \displaystyle\mathbf{h}_{\ell,t}=\Theta_{n}(1),\mathbf{h}_{\ell,t+1}-\mathbf{h}_{\ell,t}=\Theta_{n}(1),\mathcal{L}_{t+1}(\mathbf{h}_{L,t+1})-\mathcal{L}_{t}(\mathbf{h}_{L,t})=\Theta_{n}(1); (3.1) where \mathbf{h}_{\ell,t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}=\mathrm{activation}(\mathbf{W}^{\ell}_{t}\mathbf{h}_{\ell-1,t}) is the output of the \ell-th layer at step t and \mathcal{L} is the loss. 1 1 1 We consider models that are feed-forward at any local level in this work. The concrete scheme of \mu\mathsf{P} vary for different optimizers ( Chizat and Netrapalli, 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Bernstein, 2025a ) . We consider the scheme for Muon ( Bernstein, 2025a ) in this work, whose original form is often derived from the so-called spectral conditions.

sections.heading: 3.1.1 Spectral conditions
sections.text:
Since rigorous analyses under \mu\mathsf{P} by far usually resort to mathematically involved random matrix machinery, and are restricted to only a constant number of update steps ( Yang and Hu, 2021 ; Hajjar et al., 2024 ; Chizat et al., 2024 ) ; it has been attractive for practitioners to recover the scaling scheme of \mu\mathsf{P} via CLT- and LLN-type heuristics ( Yang et al., 2023 ) , among which the spectral conditions ( Yang et al., 2023 ) has been widely deemed as a necessary condition for \mu\mathsf{P} (consequently, for hyperparameter transfer). Desideratum 3.1 (Feature learning) . Let \mathbf{h}_{\ell}(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\ell}} denote the features of input \mathbf{x} at layer \ell of a neural network, and let \Delta\mathbf{h}_{\ell}(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\ell}} denote their change after a gradient step. We desire that: \displaystyle\|\mathbf{h}_{\ell}\|_{2}=\Theta(\sqrt{n_{\ell}})	ext{ and }\|\Delta\mathbf{h}_{\ell}\|_{2}=\Theta(\sqrt{n_{\ell}}),	ext{ at layers }\ell=1,\cdots,L-1. Condition 3.2 (Spectral scaling) . Consider applying update \Delta\mathbf{W}^{\ell}\in\mathbf{R}^{n_{\ell}	imes n_{\ell-1}} to the weight matrix \mathbf{W}^{\ell}\in\mathbf{R}^{n_{\ell}	imes n_{\ell-1}} in \ell-th layer. The spectral norms of \mathbf{W}^{\ell} and \Delta\mathbf{W}^{\ell} should satisfy: \displaystyle\|\mathbf{W}^{\ell}\|_{*}=\Theta\left(\sqrt{ rac{n_{\ell}}{n_{\ell-1}}}ight),~\|\Delta\mathbf{W}^{\ell}\|_{*}=\Theta\left(\sqrt{ rac{n_{\ell}}{n_{\ell-1}}}ight),~	extnormal{at layers }\ell=1,\ldots,L. Condition 3.2 implemented with \mu\mathsf{P} only guarantees the desired spectral norms of the weight \mathbf{W} and update  m{\Delta} across different widths, but not necessarily guarantees the desired spectral norms across entire time horizon of the training steps . In other words, because \mu\mathsf{P} is data-independent , the data-dependent nature of training intuitively may necessitate hard constraints for the training stability over time. In fact, Yang et al. (2023) outlined another plausible way of implementing Condition 3.2 for the standard parametrization (SP). In particular, Yang et al. (2023, Equations (16) and (17)) implement it via explicit spectral normalization as 2 2 2 We ignore the momentum here and use the raw gradient instead only to avoid notation clutter. \displaystyle m{\Delta}_{t} \displaystyle\leftarrow rac{
abla_{\mathbf{W}_{t}}\mathcal{L}_{t}}{\|
abla_{\mathbf{W}_{t}}\mathcal{L}_{t}\|},\quad\mathbf{W}_{t+ rac{1}{2}}\leftarrow\mathbf{W}_{t}-\eta\sqrt{ rac{n_{\ell}}{n_{\ell-1}}} m{\Delta}_{t},\quad\mathbf{W}_{t+1}\leftarrow\sigma\sqrt{ rac{n_{\ell}}{n_{\ell-1}}} rac{\mathbf{W}_{t+ rac{1}{2}}}{\|\mathbf{W}_{t+ rac{1}{2}}\|}. (3.2) Such a two-step spectral normalization approach for SP has a trick issue: as long as \|\mathbf{W}_{t+ rac{1}{2}}\|
eq\sqrt{n_{\ell}/n_{\ell-1}}, the normalization of weight will implicitly shrink or amplify the spectral magnitude of the previously normalized  m{\Delta}_{t} because  rac{\mathbf{W}_{t+ rac{1}{2}}}{\|\mathbf{W}_{t+ rac{1}{2}}\|}= rac{\mathbf{W}_{t}-\eta\sqrt{ rac{n_{\ell}}{n_{\ell-1}}} m{\Delta}_{t}}{\|\mathbf{W}_{t+ rac{1}{2}}\|}. Therefore, SP equipped with Equation 3.2 may not perfectly satisfy the spectral conditions for both the weight \mathbf{W}_{t+1} and the one-step neat update  m{\Delta}_{t+1} simultaneously. Similar issues also exist for the spectral normalization algorithms discussed in ( Su, 2025a ; Zhihu, 2025 ) .

sections.heading: 3.2 Muon
sections.text: The Muon optimizer ( Jordan et al., 2024a ) was proposed to leverage the 2D geometric structure of model parameter matrices during training. Given a momentum coefficient \mu\in(0,1) and a learning rate \eta_{t}>0, the update rule is defined as: \displaystyle\mathbf{M}_{t} \displaystyle=\mu\mathbf{M}_{t}+\nabla f(\mathbf{X}_{t},\bm{\xi}_{t}), \displaystyle\mathbf{O}_{t} \displaystyle=\text{NewtonSchulz}\left(\mathbf{M}_{t}\right), \displaystyle\mathbf{X}_{t+1} \displaystyle=\mathbf{X}_{t}-\eta_{t}\mathbf{O}_{t}. Here, \mathbf{X}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} is the parameter matrix, and \mathbf{M}_{t} represents the momentum matrix. The core of the update relies on the Newton-Schulz iteration ( Bernstein and Newhouse, 2024 ) , which is employed to approximate the polar factor \mathbf{U}_{t}\mathbf{V}_{t}, where \mathbf{U}_{t}\bm{\Sigma}_{t}\mathbf{V}_{t} is the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of \mathbf{M}_{t}. Moreover, instead of the original momentum \mathbf{M}_{t}, a Nesterov-style term \mu\mathbf{M}_{t}+\nabla f(\mathbf{X}_{t},\bm{\xi}_{t}) is usually used in Newton-Schulz iteration in practice. It is worth noting that Muon is designed only for matrix-shaped parameters. Vector-like parameters, including embeddings, normalization layers, and language model heads, are typically optimized by AdamW. However, empirical studies ( Yuan et al., 2025 ; Semenov et al., 2025 ) have reported that the original Muon formulation yields unsatisfactory performance in large-scale language modeling tasks. Liu et al. (2025a) identified the source of this suboptimal performance as a mismatch between the update magnitudes applied to the different parameter types. To address this disparity, they proposed a variant that rescales the Muon update to match this magnitude with a factor of 0.2\sqrt{\max(m,n)} for the weight \mathbf{X}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}. And this corrected version has demonstrated strong empirical performance on several benchmarks ( Semenov et al., 2025 ; Wen et al., 2025 ) .

sections.heading: 4.1 Formulation: Spectral conditions with spectral constraints
sections.text: Suppose \mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\ell}\times n_{\ell-1}} for the current step with a spectral norm in compliance with its spectral condition, i.e., \displaystyle\|\mathbf{W}\|=S{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\coloneqq}\sqrt{n_{\ell}/n_{\ell-1}}, which can be achieved either by \mu\mathsf{P} initialization (with high probability) or explicit normalization. Then our formulation is \displaystyle\max_{\bm{\Delta}:\|\bm{\Delta}\|\leq 1}\langle{\mathbf{G}},{\bm{\Delta}}\rangle (4.1) \displaystyle\text{ subject to }\|\mathbf{W}-\eta\cdot S\cdot\bm{\Delta}\|=S, where \mathbf{G} is usually replaced by a momentum estimator and \eta>0 is a constant step size that does not scale with the model size.

sections.heading: 4.2 A projection-based solution without spectral normalization
sections.text: For the optimization problem in ( 4.1 ), suppose the top singular value S\coloneqq\sigma_{1}(\mathbf{W}) is unique, with the corresponding left and right singular vectors \mathbf{u}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{1}; which holds almost surely for typical random weights with finite n_{\ell}\vee n_{\ell-1}. When the step size \eta satisfies \eta\cdot S\leq S-\sigma_{2}(\mathbf{W}), \bm{\Delta} does not disturb the top singular direction of \mathbf{W}, the constraint \|\mathbf{W}-\eta\cdot S\cdot\bm{\Delta}\|=S is satisfied automatically; which is rigorously justified in Section A.2 . To ensure this property, it is sufficient ( Proposition A.1 ) to have the following constraints: \displaystyle\quad\mathbf{u}_{1}^{\top}\bm{\Delta}=0,\quad\bm{\Delta}\mathbf{v}_{1}=0. (4.2) Equivalently, \bm{\Delta} must lie in the orthogonal subspace: \displaystyle\bm{\Delta}=\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{U}^{\perp}}\bm{\Delta}\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{V}^{\perp}}. (4.3) where \mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{U}^{\perp}}=\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{u}_{1}\mathbf{u}_{1}^{\top} is the projection orthogonal to \mathbf{u}_{1}, and \mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{V}^{\perp}}=\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{v}_{1}\mathbf{v}_{1}^{\top} is the projection orthogonal to \mathbf{v}_{1}. With this constraint, \mathbf{W}-\eta\cdot S\cdot\bm{\Delta} has singular value S along \mathbf{u}_{1},\mathbf{v}_{1}, while other singular values are \sigma_{i}(\mathbf{W}) perturbed by \eta\cdot S\cdot\bm{\Delta}. Since \sigma_{i}(\mathbf{W})\leq\sigma_{2}(\mathbf{W}),\forall i\geq 2, \|\bm{\Delta}\|=1 as well as |\eta S|\leq S-\sigma_{2}(\mathbf{W}), therefore, it holds that \sigma_{1}(\mathbf{W}-\eta\cdot S\cdot\bm{\Delta})=S, i.e., \|\mathbf{W}-\eta\cdot S\cdot\bm{\Delta}\|=S. Therefore, the optimization problem ( 4.1 ) is reduced to \displaystyle\max_{\bm{\Delta}:\|\bm{\Delta}\|\leq 1}\langle{\mathbf{G}},{\bm{\Delta}}\rangle (4.4) \displaystyle\text{ subject to }\mathbf{u}_{1}^{\top}\bm{\Delta}=0,\bm{\Delta}\mathbf{v}_{1}=0. By projecting the gradient matrix \mathbf{G} to the same orthogonal subspace in ( 4.3 ) to attain \widehat{\mathbf{G}}:=\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{U}^{\perp}}\mathbf{G}\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{V}^{\perp}}, ( 4.4 ) becomes: \displaystyle\max_{\bm{\Delta}:\|\bm{\Delta}\|\leq 1}\langle{\widehat{\mathbf{G}}},{\bm{\Delta}}\rangle. (4.5) And the optimal update is \bm{\Delta}=\widehat{\mathbf{U}}\widehat{\mathbf{V}}^{\top}, where \widehat{\mathbf{U}}\widehat{\bm{\Sigma}}\widehat{\mathbf{V}}^{\top}=\text{SVD}(\widehat{\mathbf{G}}) is the SVD decomposition of the projected gradient matrix. The the analysis above yields Muon++ as shown in Algorithm 1 , where \mathrm{msign}(\mathbf{W}) for some matrix \mathbf{W} with singular value decomposition of \mathbf{U},\bm{\Sigma},\mathbf{V}^{\top}=\text{SVD}(\mathbf{W}) is the matrix sign function defined as \mathrm{msign}(\mathbf{W}):=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top} ( Roberts, 1980 ; Denman and Beavers Jr, 1976 ) . Algorithm 1 Muon++ 1: input: \mathbf{W}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\ell}\times n_{\ell-1}},\mu,\{\eta_{t}\}_{\geq 1} 2: Set \mathbf{W}_{1}\leftarrow\mathbf{W}_{0} (initialized following ( Yang et al., 2023 , Parametrization 1) ), \mathbf{M}_{0}\leftarrow\mathbf{0} 3: for t=1, to T do 4: Compute gradient \mathbf{G}_{t}=\nabla f_{t}(\mathbf{W}_{t}) 5: \mathbf{M}_{t}=\mu\mathbf{M}_{t-1}+\mathbf{G}_{t} 6: Compute the top left singular vector \mathbf{u}_{1,t} and right singular vector \mathbf{v}_{1,t} of \mathbf{W}_{t} 7: \mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{U}_{t}^{\perp}}=\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{u}_{1,t}\mathbf{u}_{1,t}^{\top}, \mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{V}_{t}^{\perp}}=\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{v}_{1,t}\mathbf{v}_{1,t}^{\top} 8: \bm{\Delta}_{t}=\mathrm{msign}(\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{U}_{t}^{\perp}}\mathbf{M}_{t}\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{V}_{t}^{\perp}}) 9: \mathbf{W}_{t+1}=\mathbf{W}_{t}-\eta_{t}\cdot S\cdot\bm{\Delta}_{t} 10: end for For a sufficiently small effective learning rate \eta, the condition \eta S\leq S-\sigma_{2}(\mathbf{W}) can be satisfied with high probability. Therefore, Algorithm 1 is solid enough for training with moderately large width without explicit spectral-norm normalization, e.g., \mathtt{hidden\_size}\leq 4096. However, for weight \mathbf{W} with prohibitively large size, S-\sigma_{2}(\mathbf{W}) may vanish to zero, which motivates some practical alleviations discussed below.

sections.heading: 4.3 Practical considerations for models with ultra-large width
sections.text: Algorithm 2 Muon++ with Direct Rescaling 1: input: \mathbf{W}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{\ell}\times n_{\ell-1}},\mu,\{\eta_{t}\}_{t\geq 1} 2: Set \mathbf{W}_{1}\leftarrow\mathbf{W}_{0} (initialized following ( Yang et al., 2023 , Parametrization 1) ), \mathbf{M}_{0}\leftarrow\mathbf{0} 3: for t=1, to T do 4: Compute gradient \mathbf{G}_{t}=\nabla f_{t}(\mathbf{W}_{t}) 5: \mathbf{M}_{t}=\mu\mathbf{M}_{t-1}+\mathbf{G}_{t} 6: Compute the top left singular vector \mathbf{u}_{1,t} and right singular vector \mathbf{v}_{1,t} of \mathbf{W}_{t} 7: \mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{U}_{t}^{\perp}}=\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{u}_{1,t}\mathbf{u}_{1,t}^{\top}, \mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{V}_{t}^{\perp}}=\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{v}_{1,t}\mathbf{v}_{1,t}^{\top} 8: \bm{\Delta}_{t}=\mathrm{msign}(\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{U}_{t}^{\perp}}\mathbf{M}_{t}\mathbf{P}_{\mathbf{V}_{t}^{\perp}}) 9: \mathbf{W}_{t+\frac{1}{2}}=\mathbf{W}_{t}-\eta_{t}\cdot S\cdot\bm{\Delta}_{t} 10: \mathbf{W}_{t+1}\leftarrow S\cdot\mathbf{W}_{t+\frac{1}{2}}/\|\mathbf{W}_{t+\frac{1}{2}}\| 11: end for Given Fact A.2 that \sigma_{1}\approx\sigma_{2} for some ultra high-dimensional weight matrices under \mu\mathsf{P} scaling, Algorithm 2 may serve as an approximate relief when n_{\ell}\wedge n_{\ell-1}\gg 1, leveraging a direct spectral rescaling in 10 . It is worth noting that Algorithm 2 is equivalent to Algorithm 1 if \eta_{t}S\leq S-\sigma_{2}(\mathbf{W}_{t}) or \|\mathbf{W}_{t+1/2}\|=S (in 9 ), due to spectral cancelations between \bm{\Delta}_{t} and \mathbf{W}_{t}. Even when it is the case, if \|\mathbf{W}_{t+1/2}\| dominates \|\mathbf{W}_{t}\| by a non-negligible margin, the direct rescaling in Algorithm 2 might make \|\mathbf{W}_{t+1}-\mathbf{W}_{t}\| smaller than the desired norm of \sqrt{n_{\ell}/n_{\ell-1}} in the spectral condition of the neat update, which is not likely to hinder the training stability but may affect the perfectness of hyperparameter transfer. Therefore, Algorithm 2 can be served as an appropriate compromise between ideal principles and efficient implementations when the width is prohibitively large. Remark 4.1 . Although Fact A.2 implies that \sigma_{1}-\sigma_{2} may be small for certain \mathbf{W} with a stable rank of \Omega(n_{\ell}\wedge n_{\ell-1}) and large enough n_{\ell}\wedge n_{\ell-1}, it is worth noting that around the late stage of training (e.g., for t>T/2), (1) many relevant weights may have smaller stable ranks compared to their initialization (and thus \sigma_{1}-\sigma_{2} becomes larger with high probability), and (2) \eta_{t} will be super small if following practically favorable learning rate schedulers ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2016 ; Hu et al., 2024 ; Bergsma et al., 2025 ) . Therefore, 10 in Algorithm 2 is not likely to take place too frequently after the very first portion of the training procedure. Remark 4.2 . The conceptually standard principle for solving constrained optimization problems Equations 4.1 and 4.4 is strong duality, which we outline as another iterative alternative of Algorithms 1 and 2 under a first-order oracle premise in Appendix B .

sections.heading: 4.4 Should the spectral condition for weight matrices be time-independent?
sections.text: The S in Equation 4.1 is originally deemed to be time-independent because it is widely believed that the spectral condition S=\sqrt{n_{\ell}/n_{\ell-1}} for \mathbf{W} is crucial for preserving the norm of the feature vectors as well as their update scales ( Yang and Hu, 2021 ; Yang et al., 2023 ) . However, for the late 3 3 3 See Appendix E for an example of the late stage in LLM training (even with, e.g., Adam under \mu\mathsf{P} ). stage of training, e.g., when the number of training steps T satisfies T\gtrsim\mathrm{poly}(n_{\ell}\wedge n_{\ell-1}), Issue 1 the elements within \mathbf{W} may become mutually dependent (due to the accumulation of the impact of data-dependent gradient information), especially when the training token budget is huge yet n_{\ell} and n_{\ell-1} remain mild ; Issue 2 the activation vector \mathbf{h}^{(\ell-1)} and \mathbf{W}^{(\ell)} may correlate in an intriguing yet complex way. Remark 4.3 . Issue 2 has been empirically studied in different contexts ( Everett et al., 2024 ; Haas et al., 2025 ) . However, it is by far still hard to model it in an principled way that is easily implementable for practitioners to remedy this issue. We leave the data-dependent treatment of this issue as a future direction. Any of these two issues alone already breaks down the derivation of the spectral conditions ( Yang et al., 2023 , Condition 1) . To inspire future work on the refinement of spectral conditions, we initiate an effort on top of Algorithm 1 towards a principled treatment of Issue 1 . In detail, we introduce a minimalist correlation model for \mathbf{W}, which is promising to estimate on the fly (i.e., during the normal training procedure) efficiently. Definition 4.4 (\rho-correlated weight) . \mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} is 4 4 4 We denote m=n_{\ell} and n=n_{\ell-1} in the presentation below to avoid notation clutter. a \rho-correlated weight if \{W_{i,j}\}_{(i,j)\in[m]\times[n]}\overset{\scriptsize\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}) and \mathrm{corr}(W_{i,j},W_{k,\ell})=\rho for any i\neq j or k\neq\ell. Given \rho\geq 0, Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1), \bm{\Phi}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} with \mathrm{i.i.d.} standard Gaussian entries, and \mathbf{J}\coloneqq{\bm{1}}_{m}{\bm{1}}_{n}^{\top}, we have \sigma^{-1}\mathbf{W}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{d}}}{{=}}\sqrt{\rho}Z\mathbf{J}+\sqrt{1-\rho}\bm{\Phi} if and only if \mathbf{W} is a \rho-correlated weight. Thus, we identify \displaystyle\mathbf{W}\coloneqq\sigma\big(\sqrt{\rho}Z\mathbf{J}+\sqrt{1-\rho}\bm{\Phi}\big) (4.6) in the analysis below W.L.O.G. To further simplify the presentation, we make the following assumption, which is reasonable for many 2-dimensional weights in modern LLMs like Bi et al. (2024) . Assumption 4.5 . m/n\equiv c, where c\in(0,1] is a constant; i.e., the ratio between the input and output dimensions of \mathbf{W} is fixed. Assumption 4.5 implies \sqrt{m/n}=\sqrt{c}=\Theta(1); under which we make a further simplification that, to preserve the elementwise magnitude of the activation vector after multiplied by \mathbf{W}, it is still desired that \|\mathbf{W}\|\asymp\sqrt{c} for any large n in every iteration, i.e., Desideratum 4.6 . For the \rho-correlated weight \mathbf{W}, \|\mathbf{W}\|=\Theta_{\mathbb{P}}(1). Remark 4.7 . In the discussion above, we assume that \rho\geq 0, which is indeed a limitation. However, whenever this \rho-correlated weight is well-defined, i.e., the covariance matrix of the mn random variables in \mathbf{W} is positive semi-definite, we will always have \rho\gtrsim-(mn)^{-1}, as detailed in Section D.1 . It also implies that \rho is not very likely to be negative for relatively large n under this phenomenological model. To achieve Desideratum 4.6 , it is vital to carefully track the relative order of \sigma versus \rho in Definition 4.4 compared to n. Therefore, it is natural to index them by \sigma_{n} and \rho_{n} for the \mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} under Assumption 4.5 in the following analysis. We analyze \|\mathbf{W}\|_{F}, \|\mathbf{W}\|, and the stable rank \mathrm{srank}(\mathbf{W})\coloneqq\|\mathbf{W}\|_{F}^{2}/\|\mathbf{W}\|^{2} as follows, emphasizing their dependency on the scaling of (\rho_{n},\sigma_{n}). The regime of non-vanishing correlation is straightforward: \displaystyle\rho_{n}\asymp 1\Longrightarrow\quad\text{ \lx@cref{creftypecap~refnum}{desi:spectral-corr} is satisfied if and only iff }\sigma_{n}\asymp n^{-1}, (4.7) whose proof deferred to Section D.2 . The regime of \rho_{n}\ll 1 is more interesting as shown below. Proposition 4.8 . Under Assumption 4.5 , if \rho_{n}\ll 1, {\|\mathbf{W}\|_{F}}/\big({\sigma_{n}\sqrt{mn}}\big)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{\text{a.s.}}1. Proposition 4.8 manifests that \|\mathbf{W}\|_{F} behaves consistently in the regime of vanishing correlation, yet \|\mathbf{W}\| behaves distinctly in three different sub-regimes: \rho_{n}\ll n^{-1}, \rho_{n}\gg n^{-1}, and \rho_{n}\asymp n^{-1}. Proposition 4.9 . Under the same assumptions in Proposition 4.8 and the identification Equation 4.6 : \displaystyle\rho_{n}\ll n^{-1} \displaystyle\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{\|\mathbf{W}\|}{\sigma_{n}(\sqrt{m}+\sqrt{n})}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{\text{a.s.}}1, (4.8) \displaystyle\rho_{n}\gg n^{-1} \displaystyle\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{\|\mathbf{W}\|}{\sigma_{n}\sqrt{mn\rho_{n}}}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{\text{a.s.}}|Z|=\Theta{P}(1), (4.9) \displaystyle\rho_{n}\asymp n^{-1} \displaystyle\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{\|\mathbf{W}\|}{\sigma_{n}(\sqrt{m}+\sqrt{n})}=O{P}(1), (4.10) and in particular, when \lim_{n\to\infty}n\rho_{n}=\tau\in(0,+\infty), \displaystyle\frac{\|\mathbf{W}\|}{\sigma_{n}(\sqrt{m}+\sqrt{n})}\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{\text{a.s.}}\ind{\{Z^{2}\tau\sqrt{c}\leq 1\}}+\ind{\{Z^{2}\tau\sqrt{c}>1\}}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{(Z^{2}\tau+1)(Z^{2}\tau c+1)}}{|Z|\big(1+\sqrt{c}\big)\sqrt{\tau}}=\Theta{P}(1). (4.11) Section D.3 (resp. Section D.4 ) details the proof of Proposition 4.8 (resp. Proposition 4.9 ). The main take-away of Propositions 4.8 , 4.9 and 4.7 lies in the regime \rho_{n}\gg n^{-1}, in which we need \displaystyle{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}\sigma_{n}\asymp n^{-1}\rho_{n}^{-1/2}} (4.12) to achieve Desideratum 4.6 ; and \mathrm{srank}(\mathbf{W})=\Theta{P}(\rho_{n}^{-1}) in this case, which is smaller than the common \mathrm{srank}\sim mn/(\sqrt{m}+\sqrt{n})^{2} in the \mu\mathsf{P} literature. In contrast, in regimes of \rho_{n}\lesssim n^{-1}, Proposition 4.9 indicates that the commonly used \sigma_{n}\asymp n^{-1/2} is necessary and sufficient for Desideratum 4.6 . Therefore, as long as we can efficiently estimate \rho_{n} or its scaling exponent w.r.t. n on the fly, we may be able to adapt \mathbf{W} to its current correlation status .

sections.heading: 4.4.1 Correlation estimation and its potential utilization
sections.text: Empirically, given the weight matrix from a certain checkpoint, we can estimate \rho_{n} by the method of moments in O(mn) time as \displaystyle\widehat{\rho}_{n}^{\mathrm{MoM}}\leftarrow\frac{mn\overline{W}^{2}-\widehat{\sigma}_{n}^{2}}{(mn-1)\widehat{\sigma}_{n}^{2}}, (4.13) where \overline{W}\leftarrow(mn)^{-1}\sumop\displaylimits_{i,j}W_{i,j} and \widehat{\sigma}_{n}^{2}\leftarrow(mn)^{-1}\sumop\displaylimits_{i,j}W_{i,j}^{2}. Under the belief of \rho_{n}=1/\mathrm{poly}(n), it is possible to fit a linear regression for \log\widehat{\rho}_{n} v.s. \log n across different model widths to determine the scaling exponent of \rho_{n}. Moreover, our analysis Equation 4.12 above suggests that it is viable to introduce a threshold C such that when the estimator \widehat{\rho}_{n}^{\mathrm{MoM},(t)} Equation 4.13 for the current step t exceeds C\cdot(n^{-1/2}+m^{-1/2}) for the first time, we scale \mathbf{W}_{t} by a factor of \sqrt{\widehat{\rho}_{n}^{\mathrm{MoM},(t-1)}/\widehat{\rho}_{n}^{\mathrm{MoM},(t)}}. Remark 4.10 . The correlation utilization approach outlined above can be more computationally efficient than other iterative approaches (e.g., 10 of Algorithm 2 ) for adjusting the spectral status of \mathbf{W}_{t+1}. In particular, we recall that 10 of Algorithm 2 requires an additional invocation of power (or Lanczos) iteration because it needs the concrete spectral norm computation.

sections.heading: 5 Discussion
sections.text: Our projection-based Muon++ algorithm enforces the required spectral properties of weight matrices throughout the training process in an on-the-fly manner, without imposing overly rigid structural constraints (e.g., orthogonal rows or columns ( Bernstein, 2025b ) ). Instead, it allows learned representations to be encoded through correlated features, while still satisfying Desideratum 4.6 at each optimization step, even in the late stages of training.

sections.heading: 5.1 Relevance and limitations
sections.text: Originality and Relevance. Beyond the introduction of new algorithms, our work draws on well-established tools from the theory of Gaussian random matrices ( Benaych-Georges and Nadakuditi, 2012 ; Speicher, 2020 ) and classical point estimation methods, including the method of moments. While these techniques are independently well studied, our contribution lies in their principled integration into the study of spectral conditions under \mu\mathsf{P}, leveraging training-time information across the entire optimization process to enable practical and reliable matrix-based optimizers. Limitations. For Muon++, we still need explicit spectral normalization for super large-width cases in Algorithm 2 . Also, the modeling framework in Section 4.4 for alleviating Item Issue 1 is far from comprehensive, and a neat and sound mitigation of Item Issue 2 is left as a future work.

sections.heading: 5.2 On the impact of weight decay v.s. explicit constraints
sections.text: It is worth noticing that our norm constraint Equation 4.1 never rules out the necessity of weight decay (which is not discussed in the current manuscript), namely, weight decay is not necessarily redundant even under explicit magnitude normalization: projected gradient methods alone will converge to stationary points if certain stationary points satisfy the norm constraints, but weight decay may let the model never converge to any stationary point during pre-training even if the momentum is already near-vanishing.

sections.heading: A.3 \sigma_{1}(\mathbf{W})-\sigma_{2}(\mathbf{W}) vanishes as width goes large
sections.text: Fact A.2 (See, e.g., Bloemendal and Virág 2013, Introduction ) . Let \mathbf{A}=(A_{ij})_{(i,j)\in[m]\times[n]} be a random matrix with \mathrm{i.i.d.} real entries such that \mathbb{E}A_{11}=0, \mathbb{E}A_{11}^{2}=1, and \mathbb{E}A_{11}^{4} < \infty; suppose m/n\equiv c as n\to\infty, i.e., m/n is always a constant c that does not vary with n; let \mathbf{W}\coloneqq n^{-1/2}\mathbf{A} and \sigma_{k}\coloneqq\sigma_{k}(\mathbf{W}) be the k-th singular value of \mathbf{W}, then as n\to\infty, (\sigma_{1}-\sigma_{2})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{a.s.}}}{{\longrightarrow}}0.

sections.heading: D.2 Proof of Equation 4.7
sections.text: In this case of non-vanishing correlation, i.e., \rho_{n}\asymp 1, the pairwise weight correlation is bounded (from below) away from zero for any sufficiently large n, which is a “super”-correlated regime. Recall the identification in Section 4.4 of \sigma_{n}^{-1}\mathbf{W}\coloneqq\sqrt{\rho_{n}}Z\mathbf{J}+\sqrt{1-\rho_{n}}\bm{\Phi}, under which \displaystyle\sigma_{n}\sqrt{\rho_{n}}|Z|\|\mathbf{J}\|-\sigma_{n}\sqrt{1-\rho_{n}}\|\bm{\Phi}\|\leq\|\mathbf{W}\|\leq\sigma_{n}\sqrt{\rho_{n}}|Z|\|\mathbf{J}\|+\sigma_{n}\sqrt{1-\rho_{n}}\|\bm{\Phi}\|. Under Assumption 4.5 , \|\mathbf{J}\|=\Theta(n), and n^{-1/2}{\|\bm{\Phi}\|}\in\Theta{P}(1)\ni|Z| (again due to the classic Bai-Yin theorem, see, e.g., Speicher 2020 ); since 0 < \liminf_{n\to\infty}\rho_{n}\leq\limsup_{n\to\infty}\rho_{n}\leq 1, we conclude that: Desideratum 4.6 is satisfied if and only if \sigma_{n}\asymp n^{-1}.

sections.heading: D.3 Proof of Proposition 4.8
sections.text: We put all randomness in one probability space to establish pointwise convergence. In detail, let \{\phi_{ij}\}_{i,j\geq 1} be an (countably) infinite two-dimensional array of \mathrm{i.i.d.} random variables following \mathcal{N}(0,1). Explicitly write m_{n}\coloneqq cn and N_{n}\coloneqq m_{n}\cdot n to emphasize the dependency on n, and denote the submatrix \{\phi_{ij}\}_{1\leq i\leq m_{n},1\leq j\leq n} by \bm{\Phi}^{(n)}, and denote {\bm{1}}_{m_{n}}{\bm{1}}_{n}^{\top} by \mathbf{J}^{(n)}. Our identification Equation 4.6 thus reads \sigma_{n}^{-1}\mathbf{W}^{(n)}=\sqrt{\rho_{n}}Z\mathbf{J}^{(n)}+\sqrt{1-\rho_{n}}\bm{\Phi}^{(n)}, for which \displaystyle\frac{\|\mathbf{W}^{(n)}\|_{F}^{2}}{N_{n}\sigma_{n}^{2}} \displaystyle=\rho_{n}Z^{2}+2Z\sqrt{\rho_{n}(1-\rho_{n})}\cdot\frac{\big\langle{\mathbf{J}^{(n)}},{\bm{\Phi}^{(n)}}\big\rangle}{N_{n}}+(1-\rho_{n})\frac{\|\bm{\Phi}^{(n)}\|_{F}^{2}}{N_{n}} \displaystyle=\underbrace{\rho_{n}Z^{2}}_{\text{(i)}}+2Z\sqrt{\rho_{n}(1-\rho_{n})}\cdot\underbrace{\frac{\big\langle{\mathbf{J}^{(n)}},{\bm{\Phi}^{(n)}}\big\rangle}{N_{n}}}_{\text{(ii)}}+(1-\rho_{n})\underbrace{N_{n}^{-1}\sumop\displaylimits_{i=1}^{m_{n}}\sumop\displaylimits_{j=1}^{n}\phi_{ij}^{2}}_{\text{(iii)}}. Recall that \rho_{n}\ll 1 means \rho_{n}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle n\to\infty}}{{\longrightarrow}}0, and Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\in\Theta{P}(1). Also, the Strong Law of Large Numbers gives \text{(ii)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{a.s.}}}{{\longrightarrow}}0 and \text{(iii)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{a.s.}}}{{\longrightarrow}}1. Therefore, the continuous mapping theorem asserts that \|\mathbf{W}^{(n)}\|_{F}/\big(\sigma_{n}\sqrt{N_{n}}\big)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{a.s.}}}{{\longrightarrow}}1.

sections.heading: D.4 Proof of Proposition 4.9
sections.text: Our setup of the probability space and the premise of \rho_{n}\ll 1 are the same as those in Section D.3 . Case of \rho_{n}\ll n^{-1}. \displaystyle\frac{\mathbf{W}}{\sigma_{n}\big(\sqrt{m}+\sqrt{n}\big)} \displaystyle=Z\underbrace{\frac{\sqrt{\rho_{n}}}{\sqrt{m}+\sqrt{n}}{\bm{1}}_{m}{\bm{1}}_{n}^{\top}}_{\mathbf{A}_{n}}+\underbrace{\sqrt{1-\rho_{n}}}_{\to 1}\cdot\underbrace{\frac{\bm{\Phi}}{\sqrt{m}+\sqrt{n}}}_{\mathbf{B}_{n}}. \|{\bm{1}}_{m}{\bm{1}}_{n}^{\top}\|=\sqrt{mn} and \rho_{n}\ll n^{-1} imply \|\mathbf{A}_{n}\|\ll 1. The Bai-Yin theorem gives \|\mathbf{B}_{n}\|\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{a.s.}}}{{\longrightarrow}}1. Also, the triangle inequality asserts \displaystyle\sqrt{1-\rho_{n}}\|\mathbf{B}_{n}\|-|Z|\|\mathbf{A}_{n}\|\leq\mathrm{LHS}\leq\sqrt{1-\rho_{n}}\|\mathbf{B}_{n}\|+|Z|\|\mathbf{A}_{n}\|, for which we pass through the limit to obtain Equation 4.8 by noticing that \mathbb{P}(|Z| < \infty)=1. Case of \rho_{n}\gg n^{-1}. \displaystyle\frac{{\mathbf{W}}}{\sigma_{n}\sqrt{mn\rho_{n}}} \displaystyle=Z\cdot\frac{{\bm{1}}_{m}{\bm{1}}_{n}^{\top}}{\sqrt{mn}}+\underbrace{\sqrt{\frac{1-\rho_{n}}{\rho_{n}}}}_{\ll\sqrt{n}}\frac{\bm{\Phi}}{\sqrt{mn}}=Z\cdot\frac{{\bm{1}}_{m}{\bm{1}}_{n}^{\top}}{\sqrt{mn}}+\frac{\bm{\Phi}}{\sqrt{m}}\cdot o(1), where \|{\bm{1}}_{m}{\bm{1}}_{n}^{\top}/\sqrt{mn}\|=1, and the Bai-Yin theorem gives m^{-1/2}{\|\bm{\Phi}\|}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{a.s.}}}{{\longrightarrow}}1+c^{-1/2}. Thus, the triangle inequality yields \displaystyle|Z|-m^{-1/2}{\|\bm{\Phi}\|}\cdot o(1)\leq\mathrm{LHS}\leq|Z|+m^{-1/2}{\|\bm{\Phi}\|}\cdot o(1), for which we pass through the limit to obtain Equation 4.9 . Case of \rho_{n}\asymp n^{-1}. Equation 4.10 again follows from a standard triangle-inequality argument with \|{\bm{1}}_{m}{\bm{1}}_{n}^{\top}\|=\sqrt{mn} and the Bai-Yin theorem. For the exact result in Equation 4.11 , note that \displaystyle\frac{\mathbf{W}}{\sigma_{n}\big(\sqrt{m}+\sqrt{n}\big)} \displaystyle=\sqrt{\rho_{n}}Z\frac{{\bm{1}}_{m}{\bm{1}}_{n}^{\top}}{\sqrt{m}+\sqrt{n}}+\sqrt{1-\rho_{n}}\frac{\bm{\Phi}}{\sqrt{m}+\sqrt{n}} \displaystyle=\sqrt{1-\rho_{n}}\frac{\bm{\Phi}}{\sqrt{m}+\sqrt{n}}+\frac{Z\sqrt{n\rho_{n}}}{(1+c^{1/2})}c^{1/2}\big(m^{-1/2}{\bm{1}}_{m}\big)\big(n^{-1/2}{\bm{1}}_{n}^{\top}\big) \displaystyle=\underbrace{\sqrt{1-\rho_{n}}\frac{\bm{\Phi}}{\sqrt{m}+\sqrt{n}}}_{\mathbf{X}_{n}}+\frac{Z\sqrt{\tau}}{(1+c^{-1/2})}(mn)^{-1/2}{\bm{1}}_{m}{\bm{1}}_{n}^{\top}+\underbrace{\frac{Z\big(\sqrt{n\rho_{n}}-\sqrt{\tau}\big)}{(1+c^{-1/2})}(mn)^{-1/2}{\bm{1}}_{m}{\bm{1}}_{n}^{\top}}_{\mathbf{C}_{n}}. Since we additionally assume n\rho_{n}\to\tau\in(0,+\infty), \|\mathbf{C}_{n}\|\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{a.s.}}}{{=}}o(1). The quarter-circle law (also known as the Marchenko–Pastur Law) ( Bai and Silverstein, 2010 ) asserts that the spectral distribution of the singular values of \mathbf{X}_{n} converges weakly to \mu({\,\mathrm{d}}s) given by \displaystyle\mu({\,\mathrm{d}}s)=\frac{\sqrt{4c-\big((1+\sqrt{c})^{2}s^{2}-1-c\big)^{2}}}{\pi cs}\ind{\Big\{s\in\Big(\frac{1-\sqrt{c}}{1+\sqrt{c}},1\Big)\Big\}}{\,\mathrm{d}}s. Also note that Z is independent of \bm{\Phi} and {\bm{1}}_{m}{\bm{1}}_{n}^{\top} serves as a rank-one perturbation, a direct application of Benaych-Georges and Nadakuditi (2012, Theorem 2.8) , in particular, Benaych-Georges and Nadakuditi (2012, Section 3.1) , yields \displaystyle\mathrm{LHS}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{a.s.}}}{{\longrightarrow}}\begin{cases}1,&|Z|c^{1/4}\tau\leq 1,\\ \frac{\sqrt{(Z^{2}\tau+1)(Z^{2}\tau c+1)}}{|Z|\big(1+\sqrt{c}\big)\sqrt{\tau}},&|Z|c^{1/4}\tau>1;\end{cases} which is equivalent to Equation 4.11 .
